questions.content:
A geochemist analyses a sample of magnesium from a mineral deposit using mass spectrometry. The sample contains three isotopes: magnesium-24 (78.6%), magnesium-25 (10.1%) and magnesium-26 (11.3%). The atomic number of magnesium is 12.

(a) State the number of neutrons in an atom of magnesium-26. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the sample, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
(c) Write the electron arrangement of a magnesium ion, Mg2+, and explain why the ion has this charge. (2 marks)
(d) The Group 2 metals react with water. Calcium reacts with cold water to give bubbles of hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution. Predict how the reaction of strontium (below calcium in Group 2) with cold water would differ from that of calcium, and explain your prediction in terms of electrons. (4 marks)

(Total 10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 14 (26 - 12)
(b) [1] (24 x 78.6 + 25 x 10.1 + 26 x 11.3) / 100 (accept sum of 18.864 + 2.525 + 2.938)
[1] = 24.327
[1] 24.3 to 3 significant figures. ECF from an incorrect sum. Common error: averaging 24, 25 and 26 to get 25.0 without using abundances (0 marks for the first two marks).
(c) [1] 2,8 (accept 2.8)
[1] Magnesium atoms (2,8,2) lose their two outer electrons to gain a full outer shell, so the ion has two more protons than electrons, giving a charge of 2+.
(d) [1] Strontium reacts more vigorously / faster (more bubbles, may heat up or fizz rapidly).
[1] Strontium atoms have more electron shells, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus.
[1] The outer electrons are more shielded from the attraction of the nucleus.
[1] They are lost more easily, so strontium is more reactive. Common error: stating that strontium has more outer electrons (it has the same number, two).

questions.content:
A student compares four substances. Data are shown below.

Substance W: melting point 1410 °C; hard; does not conduct electricity as a solid or as a liquid; insoluble in water.
Substance X: melting point 714 °C; brittle; does not conduct as a solid; conducts when dissolved in water.
Substance Y: melting point -7 °C; liquid at room temperature; does not conduct electricity; low solubility in water.
Substance Z: melting point 660 °C; malleable; conducts electricity as a solid.

(a) Identify the type of structure of each substance: giant covalent, simple molecular, giant ionic or metallic. (4 marks)
(b) Explain, in terms of particles, why substance X conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not as a solid. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why substance Z is malleable. (2 marks)
(d) Magnesium chloride, MgCl2, is an ionic compound. Describe, with a labelled diagram described in words, the transfer of electrons when magnesium reacts with chlorine to form magnesium chloride. (2 marks)

(Total 10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] W giant covalent
[1] X giant ionic
[1] Y simple molecular
[1] Z metallic
(b) [1] In the solid, ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move.
[1] When dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry the charge. Common error: saying electrons move through the solution (0 marks).
(c) [1] Layers of positive metal ions can slide over each other.
[1] The delocalised electrons keep the ions bonded as the layers slide, so the structure does not break.
(d) [1] Magnesium atom transfers two electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms, forming Mg2+.
[1] Each chlorine gains one electron to form Cl- with a full outer shell of 8 electrons (2,8,8).

questions.content:
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

A technician adds 2.50 g of calcium carbonate (relative formula mass 100) to 20.0 cm3 of hydrochloric acid of concentration 2.00 mol/dm3. The carbon dioxide is collected in a gas syringe. At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies 24.0 dm3 (24 000 cm3).

(a) Calculate the amount, in moles, of calcium carbonate used. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the amount, in moles, of hydrochloric acid used. (1 mark)
(c) Show that hydrochloric acid is the limiting reactant. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the maximum volume of carbon dioxide that can be collected. (2 marks)
(e) The technician actually collects 450 cm3 of carbon dioxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (1 mark)
(f) A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its relative formula mass is 180. Determine its empirical formula and molecular formula. (5 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 2.50 / 100 = 0.0250 mol
(b) [1] 2.00 x 20.0 / 1000 = 0.0400 mol
(c) [1] 0.0250 mol CaCO3 needs 2 x 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol HCl (mole ratio 1:2)
[1] Only 0.0400 mol HCl is available, which is less than 0.0500 mol needed, so HCl is limiting.
(d) [1] Moles CO2 = 0.0400 / 2 = 0.0200 mol (ECF using the wrong limiting reactant)
[1] 0.0200 x 24 000 = 480 cm3 (accept 0.480 dm3). Common error: using 0.0250 mol of CaCO3, giving 600 cm3.
(e) [1] 450 / 480 x 100 = 93.75% (accept 93.8 or 94%)
(f) [1] Divide by relative atomic masses: C 40.0/12 = 3.33; H 6.7/1 = 6.7; O 53.3/16 = 3.33
[1] Divide by the smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2, O 1
[1] Empirical formula CH2O
[1] Empirical mass = 30; 180 / 30 = 6
[1] Molecular formula C6H12O6

questions.content:
A group of students wants to find out how temperature affects the rate of the reaction between sodium thiosulfate solution and dilute hydrochloric acid. The reaction forms a cloudy yellow precipitate of sulfur, and a toxic, irritant gas (sulfur dioxide) is also produced.

Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + S(s) + SO2(g) + H2O(l)

The students plan to place a flask over a printed cross on paper and time how long it takes for the cross to disappear from view when looking down through the mixture.

(a) State the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables for this investigation. (4 marks)
(b) Design a method the students could follow. Your method should state the equipment used, the temperatures chosen and how the data will be collected. (4 marks)
(c) Explain two safety precautions the students should take. (2 marks)
(d) Evaluate the validity and reliability of the 'disappearing cross' method and suggest one improvement that would give more precise data. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Independent variable: temperature of the reaction mixture
[1] Dependent variable: time taken for the cross to disappear (accept rate = 1 / time)
[1] Control variable 1: volume and concentration of sodium thiosulfate (any one correct)
[1] Control variable 2: volume and concentration of acid / same flask, same cross, same observer (any second correct)
(b) [1] Use measuring cylinders to measure fixed volumes (for example 50 cm3 of thiosulfate and 5 cm3 of acid) and a thermometer.
[1] At least five temperatures spanning a suitable range (for example 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 degrees C), with the thiosulfate heated in a water bath to each temperature before adding acid.
[1] Add acid, start the stopwatch, swirl and view from above until the cross disappears, then stop the stopwatch and record the temperature.
[1] Repeat each temperature at least three times and calculate a mean. Do not award if the method gives no repeats.
(c) [1] Wear eye protection (acid and sulfur products are irritants) because splashes cause eye damage.
[1] Work in a well-ventilated room / fume cupboard, or dispose of the mixture promptly, because sulfur dioxide is toxic and can trigger asthma. Accept hot water bath precautions (do not heat above 60 degrees C, use tongs) with a reason.
(d) [1] Validity or reliability judgement: the end point is subjective because it depends on the observer's judgement of when the cross disappears, which reduces reliability and accuracy (accept: temperature falls during the experiment so the independent variable is not controlled).
[1] Improvement: use a light sensor and data logger to detect the same level of transmitted light; or use the same observer; or use a thermostatically controlled water bath. Common error: suggesting 'repeat more times' only, which does not address the subjective end point.

questions.content:
A student investigates the reaction of 0.070 g of magnesium ribbon with an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid in two experiments that differ only in temperature. The volume of hydrogen gas collected is recorded.

Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2

Experiment 1 (25 degrees C): volume of hydrogen (cm3) at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 seconds = 0, 28, 46, 58, 66, 70, 70.
Experiment 2 (40 degrees C): volume of hydrogen (cm3) at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 seconds = 0, 45, 63, 70, 70, 70, 70.

(a) Describe the shape of the graph of volume against time for Experiment 1. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the mean rate of reaction in Experiment 1 between 0 and 30 s, and between 60 and 90 s. Give units. (3 marks)
(c) Explain, using collision theory, why the rate in Experiment 1 changes with time. (3 marks)
(d) Compare Experiment 2 with Experiment 1 in terms of the initial rate and the final volume, and explain each observation. (4 marks)
(e) Verify that the final volume is consistent with 0.070 g of magnesium (relative atomic mass 24) and 24 000 cm3 per mole of gas. (2 marks)

(Total 14 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] The graph slopes steeply at first and the gradient decreases (curve gets shallower) over time.
[1] It levels off to a horizontal line at 70 cm3 from about 150 s, when the reaction is complete.
(b) [1] 0-30 s: 28 / 30 = 0.93 cm3/s
[1] 60-90 s: (58 - 46) / 30 = 0.40 cm3/s
[1] Correct units cm3/s on both answers. Common error: dividing by 90 or by the final time rather than the interval.
(c) [1] The rate decreases as the reaction proceeds because acid particles are used up so their concentration falls.
[1] Fewer particles per unit volume means fewer collisions per second.
[1] So fewer successful collisions (with at least the activation energy) occur per second, giving a lower rate. Rate falls to zero when the magnesium is used up.
(d) [1] Initial rate is higher in Experiment 2 (45 / 30 = 1.5 cm3/s compared with 0.93 cm3/s).
[1] Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy so they move faster and collide more frequently, and a greater proportion have energy of at least the activation energy.
[1] The final volume is the same (70 cm3).
[1] The same mass of magnesium (the limiting reactant) was used, so the same amount of hydrogen forms; temperature does not change the amount of product.
(e) [1] Moles Mg = 0.070 / 24 = 0.00292 mol, so moles H2 = 0.00292 mol
[1] 0.00292 x 24 000 = 70 cm3, which matches the measured final volume.

questions.content:
A student measures the energy released when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution. She mixes 50.0 cm3 of hydrochloric acid of concentration 1.00 mol/dm3 with 50.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 1.00 mol/dm3 in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the mixture rises by 6.8 degrees C. Assume the density of the solution is 1.00 g/cm3 and the specific heat capacity is 4.18 J/g/degree C.

(a) Calculate the energy transferred to the solution. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the amount, in moles, of water formed. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the enthalpy change per mole of water formed, giving the sign and units, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. (3 marks)
(d) The data book value for this reaction is -57.1 kJ/mol. Evaluate the experimental procedure by suggesting two sources of error and a modification for each. (4 marks)
(e) Methane burns: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Use the bond energies C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805 and O-H 464 kJ/mol to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Mass = 100 g (50.0 + 50.0)
[1] q = 100 x 4.18 x 6.8 = 2842.4 J (accept 2840 J or 2.84 kJ)
(b) [1] 1.00 x 50.0 / 1000 = 0.0500 mol
(c) [1] 2842.4 / 0.0500 = 56 848 J/mol = 56.8 kJ/mol (ECF from (a) and (b))
[1] Negative sign: -56.8 kJ/mol
[1] Exothermic because energy is released to the surroundings and the temperature rose.
(d) [1] Source of error: heat lost to the surroundings and air, so the temperature rise is smaller than it should be (explains the experimental value being slightly less negative).
[1] Modification: use a lid and insulation, or a better calorimeter.
[1] Source of error: the thermometer is read to +/- 0.5 degrees C, which is a large uncertainty on a 6.8 degrees C rise; or the maximum temperature is not clearly found.
[1] Modification: use a digital thermometer or data logger, plot a temperature-time graph and extrapolate to find the maximum.
(e) [1] Energy to break bonds = 4 x 413 + 2 x 498 = 2648 kJ; energy released making bonds = 2 x 805 + 4 x 464 = 3466 kJ
[1] Enthalpy change = 2648 - 3466 = -818 kJ/mol. Common error: reversing the subtraction to give +818.

questions.content:
A student carries out a titration to find the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution. She uses a pipette to place 25.0 cm3 of the sodium hydroxide solution in a flask, adds a few drops of phenolphthalein indicator, and adds hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm3 from a burette.

Titration results (cm3): rough 24.10; trial 1 22.45; trial 2 22.50; trial 3 22.55.

NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O

(a) State the colour change of phenolphthalein at the end point. (1 mark)
(b) Explain why the rough titre is not used when calculating the mean. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the mean titre and the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm3. (4 marks)
(d) A solution of hydrochloric acid and a solution of ethanoic acid both have a concentration of 0.100 mol/dm3. The pH of the hydrochloric acid is 1 and the pH of the ethanoic acid is 2.9. Explain this difference. (3 marks)
(e) Predict the pH change if the hydrochloric acid is diluted by a factor of ten and explain the change. (3 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Pink to colourless (accept: from pink to colourless as acid is added)
(b) [1] The rough titre is only an approximate value found by adding acid quickly, so it is less precise and not concordant with the others.
(c) [1] Mean = (22.45 + 22.50 + 22.55) / 3 = 22.50 cm3
[1] Moles HCl = 0.100 x 22.50 / 1000 = 0.00225 mol
[1] Mole ratio 1:1 so moles NaOH = 0.00225 mol
[1] Concentration = 0.00225 / 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm3. Common error: using 1000 / 25.0 incorrectly or forgetting to convert cm3 to dm3 (lose the relevant mark only).
(d) [1] Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid: it ionises completely in water.
[1] Ethanoic acid is a weak acid: it only partially ionises, so fewer hydrogen ions are produced.
[1] A lower hydrogen ion concentration gives a higher pH (2.9 compared with 1).
(e) [1] pH increases by 1 (to pH 2).
[1] The hydrogen ion concentration falls by a factor of ten.
[1] Each pH unit represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

questions.content:
A student tests four metals W, X, Y and Z (not their real symbols) by placing each in solutions of the sulfates of the other metals and observing whether a displacement reaction occurs. A tick means a reaction takes place.

W metal in X sulfate: tick; W in Y sulfate: tick; W in Z sulfate: tick
X metal in W sulfate: no reaction; X in Y sulfate: tick; X in Z sulfate: tick
Y metal in W sulfate: no reaction; Y in X sulfate: no reaction; Y in Z sulfate: tick
Z metal in W sulfate: no reaction; Z in X sulfate: no reaction; Z in Y sulfate: no reaction

(a) Put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (2 marks)
(b) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with copper(II) sulfate solution and state what is oxidised. (3 marks)
(c) Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr2, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode and write the half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode. (3 marks)
(d) Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon, whereas iron is extracted by heating with carbon. (2 marks)
(e) Predict the products at each electrode when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes, and explain why the blue colour of the solution stays the same. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Order W > X > Y > Z in which the most reactive metal displaces all the others.
[1] Reasoning is consistent with the table: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its solution (accept 1 mark for one adjacent pair reversed).
(b) [1] Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
[1] Magnesium atoms lose electrons: magnesium is oxidised (accept: Mg is the reducing agent).
[1] Copper ions gain electrons and are reduced. Do not accept unbalanced charges.
(c) [1] Negative electrode (cathode): lead
[1] Positive electrode (anode): bromine
[1] Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb. Common error: writing the half-equation for bromide ions at the cathode.
(d) [1] Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide.
[1] Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can reduce iron(III) oxide, which is cheaper than electrolysis.
(e) [1] Cathode: copper is deposited (mass increases); anode: copper dissolves (mass decreases).
[1] The concentration of Cu2+ ions stays constant because the number of copper ions forming at the anode equals the number removed at the cathode.

questions.content:
Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. The larger hydrocarbon molecules obtained are cracked to produce smaller, more useful molecules. One cracking reaction is:

C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4

(a) Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions. (3 marks)
(b) State the general formula of the alkenes and describe a chemical test to show that C2H4 is an alkene. (2 marks)
(c) Draw the structure of ethene in words and describe how poly(ethene) forms from ethene, including a balanced description of the repeat unit. (2 marks)
(d) A student claims: 'C8H18 and C2H4 are both hydrocarbons, so they will both burn to produce only carbon dioxide and water.' Evaluate this claim. (3 marks)

(Total 10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] The crude oil is heated and vaporised, then enters a column that is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
[1] Hydrocarbons rise until they reach a temperature below their boiling point, then condense; small molecules with low boiling points reach the top.
[1] Separation depends on boiling point, which increases with the size of the molecule because the intermolecular forces are stronger.
(b) [1] General formula CnH2n
[1] Test: add bromine water; an alkene decolourises it from orange/brown to colourless because of the C=C double bond (do not accept 'clear' for colourless).
(c) [1] Ethene is a two-carbon molecule with a C=C double bond, CH2=CH2.
[1] In addition polymerisation the double bonds open and many ethene molecules join to make a long chain, repeat unit -CH2-CH2-; no other product forms.
(d) [1] The claim is correct in complete combustion with plenty of oxygen, forming only carbon dioxide and water.
[1] In a limited supply of oxygen incomplete combustion occurs, giving carbon monoxide and soot (carbon) as well.
[1] Alkenes such as ethene have a higher proportion of carbon, so they burn with a smokier flame; the claim is therefore only valid for complete combustion.

questions.content:
A city council is deciding whether to replace its petrol buses with hydrogen fuel cell buses. The council receives the following information.

Petrol (octane, C8H18): energy released 48 MJ per kg; burns as 2C8H18 + 25O2 -> 16CO2 + 18H2O.
Hydrogen: energy released 142 MJ per kg; the only product when used in a fuel cell is water.
Most hydrogen is currently made from natural gas by steam reforming: CH4 + 2H2O -> CO2 + 4H2.
Relative atomic masses: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16. One mole of CO2 has a mass of 44 g.

(a) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 1.00 kg of octane (relative formula mass 114) burns completely. (3 marks)
(b) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when enough steam reforming is carried out to make 1.00 kg of hydrogen. (3 marks)
(c) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released per MJ of energy for each fuel, using your answers to (a) and (b), and comment on the comparison. (2 marks)
(d) Evaluate the council's decision to switch to hydrogen buses. Use your results and consider the limitations of the data, the source of hydrogen and impacts on the environment, the economy and society. (4 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Moles octane = 1000 / 114 = 8.77 mol
[1] Moles CO2 = 8.77 x 8 = 70.2 mol (ratio 2 : 16)
[1] Mass CO2 = 70.2 x 44 = 3088 g = 3.09 kg. Common error: using the ratio 1:1 (0 for the second and third marks).
(b) [1] Moles H2 = 1000 / 2 = 500 mol
[1] Moles CO2 = 500 / 4 = 125 mol (ratio 1 : 4)
[1] Mass CO2 = 125 x 44 = 5500 g = 5.5 kg
(c) [1] Petrol: 3.09 / 48 = 0.064 kg per MJ; hydrogen: 5.5 / 142 = 0.039 kg per MJ (ECF)
[1] Hydrogen made by steam reforming produces about 40% less carbon dioxide per MJ than petrol, but still emits carbon dioxide at the production stage.
(d) [1] Environmental: hydrogen buses reduce air pollution in the city (no exhaust CO2, particulates or nitrogen oxides), and the CO2 per MJ is lower, but the emissions occur at the hydrogen plant; green hydrogen from electrolysis using renewable electricity or carbon capture would reduce this.
[1] Economic: cost of the buses, fuelling stations and hydrogen is high; savings from lower fuel imports or health care costs may offset this.
[1] Limitations: data are for complete reaction at 100% efficiency, ignore transport, compression, storage and leaks, and the energy used to make the buses; the figures are only per kg and not a full life cycle assessment.
[1] Justified judgement such as: switching is beneficial in the long term if hydrogen is produced with low-carbon methods, but a pilot with a limited number of buses should be tested first. Award for a conclusion supported by data and balanced consideration of both views.
